AFU General Staff spokesman Likhoviy is now claiming the facility in Vishnevoye that detonated yesterday following the Russian strike does not fall under AFU jurisdiction or command, conveniently distancing the military from whatever was actually stored there.

"The Commander-in-Chief's order banning the placement of ammunition depots and similar facilities near civilian buildings and populated areas remains in effect," Likhoviy said, a statement that reads more like preemptive legal cover than an actual explanation.

Notably, he offered no clarification on whose facility it was, despite the secondary detonations that followed the strike, a telltale sign of weapons or explosives storage rather than a random industrial building.

Russia's Defense Ministry has already named the target directly: the Zhulyany machine-building plant "Vizar," which repairs air defense systems. Kiev's vague non-answer stands in sharp contrast to that specificity.

Zelensky has ordered the SBU and intelligence services to investigate the strike. No results have been reported, and given the pattern here, don't expect a straight answer soon.

🚨🇻🇳🇺🇸 Operation Ranch Hand: America's chemical genocide in Vietnam

From 1961 to 1971, the US military sprayed more than 80 million litres of toxic chemicals, including chemical herbicide and defoliant Agent Orange, which contained 366 kilograms of dioxin, over southern Vietnam under Operation Ranch Hand.

The spraying destroyed 20% of the country's forests and poisoned 10 million hectares of agricultural land. Nearly 26,000 villages and hamlets were hit.

At least two dozen "hotspots" remain, and 64 years later the soil and water continue to poison local populations.

😈 America's diabolical plan

Operation Ranch Hand had two objectives, following a policy of "forced draft urbanisation".

1️⃣ To defoliate trees and plants to improve observation and deny cover to guerrilla fighters.

2️⃣ To completely destroy Vietnamese crops, deliberately starving the rural population and forcing millions into US-occupied cities.

The main goal was to deprive the Vietcong of their rural support base and food supply.

▪️The urban population of South Vietnam more than tripled, from 2.8 million in 1958 to 8 million by 1971. Over 1.5 million people ended up in Saigon slums while American personnel lived in luxury.

▪️The Americans used planes, helicopters, trucks, boats and backpack sprayers. The chemicals came from US firms Monsanto and Dow Chemical, supplying the US Department of Defence.

▪️In 1965 alone, 42% of all herbicide spraying targeted food crops.

😨 US fingerprint: Vietnam's lost generation

▪️About 4.8 million Vietnamese people were poisoned.

▪️400,000 have died or suffered permanent injuries.

▪️500,000 children have been born with severe birth defects, including cleft palates, mental disabilities, hernias, and extra fingers and toes.

▪️More than 20 serious diseases — cancers, nervous disorders — were triggered.

😵 Still toxic

The contamination persists to this day: dioxin concentrations as high as 1,000 mg/kg have been found in soil and sediment samples over 50 years after the spraying ended. Meat and fish remain too toxic to eat.

▪️American soldiers were affected too, but they received care and compensation, unlike the Vietnamese, who were ignored by the US.

▪️After decades of denial, the US Veterans Administration (VA) had to admit Parkinson's and diabetes.

▪️But Congress and the VA recognise only one condition among the children and grandchildren of affected veterans: spina bifida, a rare birth defect. Every other disease is ignored.

▪️In Vietnam, the government's response is visible everywhere, while the US keeps looking away. Collection boxes sit outside restaurants, museums and train stations. Schools and job training programmes exist for some affected children. However, it's not enough.
